alabama.aging_out_age: No youth ages out of Alabama foster care before age 19, and all youth age out by their 21st birthday, under Ala. Code § 38-7-2(1) and Ala. Admin. Code r. 660-5-48-.05. The juvenile court keeps jurisdiction over a child until age 21 under Ala. Code § 12-15-117(a).
alabama.become_foster_parent: Contact the Alabama Department of Human Resources through its online foster care inquiry form or your county DHR office to start. Applicants must be at least 19, pass criminal background checks, complete a home study, and finish 30 hours of Trauma Informed Partnering for Permanence and Safety (TIPPS) training.
alabama.benefits_after: Youth who age out can get help from DHR's Independent Living Program, which offers transitional and independent living placements, life-skills training, and education and employment support up to age 21. Former foster youth can keep Medicaid coverage until age 26, can apply for Education and Training Vouchers for college or job training, and may qualify for Foster Youth to Independence (FYI) housing vouchers through DHR.
alabama.extended_care: Yes. Youth may stay in DHR care until age 21, and youth ages 18 to 20 who already left care may ask to re-enter before age 21 if they are living in a situation that poses an identifiable risk of harm. To stay in an independent or transitional living placement, a youth must work full or part time and be in a diploma, GED, or vocational program.
alabama.foster_overview: When a court finds a child cannot safely stay at home, the Alabama Department of Human Resources (DHR) takes custody and places the child in a foster home, with relatives, or in a group setting. Foster parents give the child a safe, stable home and daily care while DHR works with the birth family toward reunification or another permanent plan.
alabama.kinship_care: Yes. Under Ala. Code § 38-12-2, DHR must try to place a removed child with a relative first, and approved kinship foster parents can receive the full foster care rate. Relatives who foster for at least six months may also become kinship guardians and receive guardianship assistance.

alaska.agency_name: Alaska Department of Family and Community Services, Office of Children's Services (OCS)
alaska.aging_out_age: Youth generally age out of Alaska foster care at 18, when state custody normally ends. Under Alaska Stat. § 47.10.080, the court may extend custody one year at a time past 18, up to the 21st birthday, if continued custody is in the young person's best interests and the young person consents.
alaska.become_foster_parent: Contact the Office of Children's Services or the Alaska Center for Resource Families to start; applicants apply through OCS and work with a licensing worker. Applicants must be at least 21, pass background checks for all household members age 16 and older, complete required training, and pass a home safety inspection.
alaska.benefits_after: OCS's Independent Living Program serves youth in care from age 16 and former foster youth up to age 21 with life-skills training, education and job help, and housing support. The Foster Care Transition Program can help with education and vocational training, housing and utility assistance, career and employment services, and mentoring, and former foster youth can keep Medicaid until age 26 and apply for Education and Training Vouchers for college or job training.
alaska.extended_care: Yes. A young person who was in state custody at 18 may stay in care or ask the court to resume custody up to age 21, and must consent and sign a custody resumption agreement that includes actively working on a transition plan. Alaska also runs a Foster Care Transition Program under Alaska Stat. §§ 47.18.300-47.18.390 for young adults ages 18 to 21 who turned 18 in foster care.
alaska.foster_overview: When a child cannot safely live at home, the Alaska Office of Children's Services (OCS) places the child in temporary care with a licensed foster (resource) family, a relative, or another approved home. Foster parents provide a safe, stable, nurturing home and work with OCS and the birth family toward reunification or another permanent plan.
alaska.kinship_care: Yes. OCS looks for extended family or relatives first when a child needs out-of-home care, and relatives may be licensed foster parents or provide unlicensed relative care. Relatives must pass a criminal history screening, complete a relative study, and meet basic home safety standards, and the Alaska Center for Resource Families offers relative caregiver training and support.

arizona.aging_out_age: Youth age out of Arizona foster care at 18, when they may choose to leave care or stay. Under A.R.S. § 8-521.02, a youth who was in DCS custody as a dependent child at 18 can then choose extended foster care up to age 21.
arizona.become_foster_parent: Contact the Arizona Department of Child Safety or one of its contracted licensing agencies to start; DCS contracts with private agencies to train, license, and supervise foster families. Applicants must be at least 21, pass FBI and local background checks and get a Level One Fingerprint Clearance Card, complete pre-service training, and pass a home study and home safety inspection.
arizona.benefits_after: Youth who turn 18 in Arizona foster care are pre-enrolled in AHCCCS (Arizona Medicaid) through Young Adult Transitional Insurance, which has no income limit and runs until age 26. Former foster youth under 21 who were in foster care at age 16 or older can get Education and Training Voucher (ETV) funds for college or job training, and youth who leave at 18 can get aftercare help through the Transitional Independent Living Program (TILP), including help returning to care any time before age 21.
arizona.extended_care: Yes. Youth who turned 18 in DCS custody can stay in care voluntarily until age 21 by signing a voluntary extended foster care agreement and living in a DCS-approved supervised setting. They must also be finishing high school or a GED, enrolled in college or job training, working at least 80 hours a month, in a program that removes barriers to employment, or unable to do those things because of a documented medical condition.
arizona.foster_overview: When a court finds a child cannot safely stay at home, the Arizona Department of Child Safety (DCS) places the child in a foster home, with relatives, or in a group setting, and the state is usually the child's legal guardian. Foster parents provide a temporary home and meet the child's daily, physical, developmental, and emotional needs while DCS works toward reunification.
arizona.kinship_care: Yes. Under A.R.S. § 8-514, DCS must place a child with a parent first, then a grandparent, then kinship care with another family member or a person with a significant relationship to the child, before non-relative foster care. A kinship foster parent must be at least 18, apply with DCS, pass criminal and central registry checks, and have a home visit; kinship caregivers who become licensed receive the same foster care payment as non-relative foster parents.

arkansas.agency_name: Arkansas Department of Human Services, Division of Children and Family Services (DCFS)
arkansas.aging_out_age: Youth age out of Arkansas foster care at 18, the legal age of majority. Under Ark. Code § 9-28-114 and 9 CAR § 40-905, youth who were in foster care at 18 may choose extended foster care up to age 21.
arkansas.become_foster_parent: Submit an inquiry through Every Child Arkansas, the state's foster family network, or contact your local DCFS office; DCFS or a private licensed placement agency approves the home. Applicants must be at least 21, pass background checks, complete about 30 hours of pre-service training plus CPR and first aid, and complete a home study and home inspection.
arkansas.benefits_after: Youth who leave care at 18 can still get help from DCFS Transitional Youth Services, including help paying for school or job training, and Foster Youth to Independence (FYI) Housing Choice Vouchers are available in some counties for young adults ages 18 to 24. Former foster youth can keep Medicaid until age 26, and Education and Training Vouchers can help pay for college or vocational training.
arkansas.extended_care: Yes. Youth ages 18 to 21 who were adjudicated dependent or dependent-neglected and were in foster care at 18 may choose the Extended Foster Care Program, which gives case management and help with room and board costs. To stay, the youth must be finishing high school or a GED, enrolled in college or vocational school, in a program that promotes employment, working at least 80 hours a month, have a viable plan to meet one of those, or be unable to do them because of a documented medical condition.
arkansas.foster_overview: When a court finds a child cannot safely stay at home, the Arkansas Division of Children and Family Services (DCFS), part of the Department of Human Services, places the child in a foster (resource) home, with relatives, or in another approved setting. Foster parents give the child a safe, stable home and daily care while DCFS works with the birth family toward reunification or another permanent plan.
arkansas.kinship_care: Yes. Under 9 CAR § 40-708, DCFS treats safe and appropriate relatives and fictive kin as the best placements and gives them preferential consideration, aiming for a child's first placement to be with a relative when possible. Relatives can open as provisional resource homes and receive support payments while working toward full approval, and relatives caring for children outside the foster care system may qualify for the Kinship Care Subsidy Program.

california.aging_out_age: Youth age out of California foster care at 18, when juvenile court dependency normally ends. Under Assembly Bill 12 (AB 12), the California Fostering Connections to Success Act, eligible youth can instead stay in care as nonminor dependents until age 21.
california.become_foster_parent: Contact your county child welfare agency or a licensed Foster Family Agency to start California's single Resource Family Approval (RFA) process, which covers fostering, adoption, and guardianship. Applicants must be at least 18, pass criminal background checks, complete at least 12 hours of pre-approval training, and pass a home environment assessment.
california.benefits_after: Youth in Extended Foster Care keep foster care payments, Medi-Cal health coverage, and case management, and youth who leave at 18 can re-enter before age 21 through a Voluntary Re-Entry Agreement. After care ends, former foster youth can keep Medi-Cal until age 26, get Education and Training Vouchers for college or job training, and may qualify for THP-Plus transitional housing and support services up to age 24, or 25 in counties that extended the program.
california.extended_care: Yes. Under AB 12, youth who had a foster care placement order on their 18th birthday can remain in Extended Foster Care until age 21 by signing a Mutual Agreement for Extended Foster Care (form SOC 162). They must meet one of five participation rules: be in high school or a GED program, be in college or vocational school, work at least 80 hours a month, be in a program that helps them find work or remove barriers to work, or be unable to do those things because of a medical or mental health condition.
california.foster_overview: When a juvenile court finds a child cannot safely stay at home, the county child welfare agency, overseen by the California Department of Social Services (CDSS), places the child with an approved resource family, a relative, or in another licensed setting. Resource families provide a safe home and daily care while the county works with the birth family toward reunification or another permanent plan.
california.kinship_care: Yes. Relatives and nonrelative extended family members get preferential consideration for placement, and they go through the same Resource Family Approval process as other foster parents. Relatives who become legal guardians can receive Kinship Guardianship Assistance Payments (Kin-GAP), which AB 12 extended up to age 21 for eligible youth.

colorado.aging_out_age: Youth generally age out of Colorado foster care at 18, and the juvenile court's jurisdiction normally continues only until age 18 and a half under Colo. Rev. Stat. § 19-3-205. The court can keep jurisdiction until age 21 for youth who are not ready for independence or who are transitioning into adult disability services.
colorado.become_foster_parent: Contact your local county department of human services or a child placement agency, or start through CO4Kids, the CDHS statewide foster care initiative, and attend an information meeting. Applicants must be at least 21, pass background checks, complete 12 hours of core training plus 27 hours of pre-certification training and CPR and first aid, and complete a home study.
colorado.benefits_after: Colorado's Chafee program helps youth currently and formerly in foster care with education, employment, housing, and life skills, and Chafee services can run up to age 23. Former foster youth can keep Medicaid until age 26, apply for Education and Training Vouchers of up to $5,000 a year for college or job training, and get help through the Colorado Fostering Success Voucher Program for housing.
colorado.extended_care: Yes. Under House Bill 21-1094, the Foster Youth in Transition program lets eligible youth voluntarily keep receiving child welfare services until the last day of the month of their 21st birthday through a voluntary services agreement with the county. To qualify, a youth must be finishing high school or a GED, enrolled in college or career and technical education, in a program that promotes or removes barriers to employment, working at least 80 hours a month, or unable to do those things because of a medical condition.
colorado.foster_overview: When a court finds a child cannot safely stay at home, the county department of human or social services places the child in a foster home, with relatives, or in another approved setting, with the Colorado Department of Human Services (CDHS) overseeing the system statewide. Foster parents provide a safe, temporary home and daily care while the county works with the birth family toward reunification or another permanent plan.
colorado.kinship_care: Yes. Relatives, friends, neighbors, and others with a significant relationship to the child can care for the child as kinship caregivers, and certified kinship foster homes receive the same daily payment as other foster homes. Colorado also runs the Colorado Kinnected navigator program for kinship families and a Kinship Adoption Program that offers free legal help with adoption for kinship caregivers in the metro Denver area.

connecticut.agency_name: Connecticut Department of Children and Families (DCF)
connecticut.aging_out_age: Youth age out of Connecticut foster care at 18, when DCF custody normally ends. Under Conn. Gen. Stat. § 17a-11, a young person who was under DCF care at 18 may voluntarily stay under DCF supervision until age 21 if DCF decides further care would help.
connecticut.become_foster_parent: Contact the Connecticut Department of Children and Families or its partner, the Connecticut Alliance of Foster and Adoptive Families, to submit an inquiry and attend an information session. Applicants must be at least 21, pass federal, state, and local criminal history and DMV checks, complete about 30 hours of pre-licensing training, and complete a home study; licensing usually takes four months or more.
connecticut.benefits_after: Youth who age out can get help with housing through DCF's Community Housing Assistance Program (CHAP) and Community Housing Employment Enrichment Resources (CHEER), plus education help through the Education and Training Voucher program and DCF post-secondary education assistance. Former foster youth can keep Medicaid coverage, and Chafee independent living services can run up to age 23; youth adopted from DCF care may get college help through DCF up to the semester of their 23rd birthday.
connecticut.extended_care: Yes. Youth who were committed to DCF as abused, neglected, or uncared for at 18 can stay voluntarily in DCF's Services Post-Majority program until age 21, with a written care plan and regular reviews. To stay, they must be finishing high school or a GED, enrolled full time in college or vocational school, or participating full time in a program that promotes or removes barriers to employment, though the commissioner can waive these rules for compelling reasons.
connecticut.foster_overview: When a court finds a child cannot safely stay at home, the Connecticut Department of Children and Families (DCF) takes custody and places the child in a licensed foster home, with relatives, or in another approved setting. Foster parents provide a safe, loving home and daily care while DCF works with the birth family toward reunification, usually aiming to reunify within 12 months.
connecticut.kinship_care: Yes. DCF must work to identify adult relatives of children in its care, and a relative can be placed with the child on an emergency basis while completing licensing, then receive the same foster care payment as a non-relative foster parent. After a relative has fostered a child for at least 12 months, the relative can ask DCF to transfer guardianship and receive a subsidized guardianship payment.

delaware.agency_name: Delaware Department of Services for Children, Youth and Their Families (DSCYF), Division of Family Services
delaware.aging_out_age: Youth age out of Delaware foster care at 18, when they leave DFS custody. Under 29 Del. Code § 9015(f), DSCYF can still fund foster care supports, housing help, and stipends for young adults ages 18 to 21, and transitional and independent living services now run to age 23.
delaware.become_foster_parent: Contact the Division of Family Services Foster Care Program through DSCYF and attend a free 3-hour foster parent information session as the first step. Applicants must be at least 21, pass fingerprint-based criminal background checks, complete about 27 hours of PRIDE pre-service training, and complete a home study and home assessment.
delaware.benefits_after: Youth who age out at 18 can get voluntary transitional and independent living services to age 23, including life-skills training, mentoring, tuition help, transitional housing support, and need-based stipends through the ASSIST program. Former foster youth can keep Medicaid until age 26 and apply for Education and Training Vouchers for college or job training.
delaware.extended_care: Delaware does not have a traditional extended foster care placement program that keeps youth in a foster home to age 21. Instead, under 29 Del. Code § 9015(f), DSCYF funds housing-related foster care supports, direct youth stipends through the ASSIST program (Achieving Self Sufficiency and Independence through Supported Transition), and independent living services for youth ages 18 to 21, and House Bill 271 (2022) extended transitional and independent living services to age 23.
delaware.foster_overview: When a court finds a child cannot safely stay at home, the Delaware Division of Family Services (DFS), part of the Department of Services for Children, Youth and Their Families (DSCYF), places the child in a foster home, with relatives, or in another approved setting. Foster parents provide a safe, secure, and stable home and daily care while DFS works with the birth family toward reunification or another permanent plan.
delaware.kinship_care: Yes. Delaware's Kinship Care Program under 31 Del. Code § 356 promotes placing children with relatives when a child needs out-of-home care, and relatives within the fifth degree of kinship can get kinship care benefits, a one-time emergency subsidy, and help through the Delaware Helpline. Relatives can also become licensed foster parents under the same standards and at the same payment rate as non-relative foster parents, or seek permanent guardianship through Family Court.

florida.agency_name: Florida Department of Children and Families (DCF)
florida.aging_out_age: Youth age out of Florida foster care at 18, when they would normally leave licensed care. Under Fla. Stat. § 39.6251, a young adult living in licensed care on their 18th birthday who has not reached permanency can choose to stay in care until age 21, or age 22 with a documented disability.
florida.become_foster_parent: Contact Florida's Foster Information Center or your local community-based care lead agency, which handles licensing in your county. Applicants must be at least 21, attend an orientation, complete at least 21 hours of free pre-service training, pass fingerprint-based criminal background checks, and pass a home inspection and home study.
florida.benefits_after: Florida's Independent Living programs include Extended Foster Care, Postsecondary Education Services and Support (PESS), which pays a monthly stipend of $1,720 to eligible youth in college or vocational school, and Aftercare Services for young adults up to age 23. Former foster youth can keep Medicaid until age 26, and Education and Training Voucher funds can help with college or job training costs.
florida.extended_care: Yes. Under Fla. Stat. § 39.6251, young adults ages 18 to 21 who turned 18 in licensed care can stay in Extended Foster Care in a supervised living setting approved by DCF or the lead agency, such as a foster home, group home, college dorm, shared housing, or apartment. To stay, they must be finishing high school or a GED, enrolled in college or vocational school, in a program that promotes or removes barriers to employment, working at least 80 hours a month, or unable to do those things because of a physical, intellectual, emotional, or psychiatric condition.
florida.foster_overview: When a court finds a child cannot safely stay at home, the Florida Department of Children and Families (DCF) places the child in licensed care through a local community-based care lead agency. Foster parents, called out-of-home caregivers, provide a safe home and daily care while the agency works with the birth family toward reunification or another permanent plan.
florida.kinship_care: Yes. Relatives, nonrelatives, and fictive kin with an existing relationship to the child can seek Level I child-specific foster home licensure, which is designed for family or like-family caregivers. Relatives caring for a dependent child may also get help through Florida's Relative Caregiver Program under Fla. Stat. § 39.5085, which pays a monthly benefit and covers the child under Medicaid.

georgia.agency_name: Georgia Department of Human Services, Division of Family and Children Services (DFCS)
georgia.aging_out_age: Youth age out of Georgia foster care at 18, when they may choose to leave care or stay. Under O.C.G.A. § 15-11-340, youth ages 18 to 21 can receive extended-care youth services through DFCS's Extended Youth Support Services (EYSS) program, known as Connected by 21.
georgia.become_foster_parent: Contact the Georgia Division of Family and Children Services or one of its more than 100 Child Placing Agencies to start; DFCS first completes a virtual information session with interested families. Applicants must be at least 21, complete pre-service training and a medical exam, pass child protective screenings and criminal record checks, and show proof of residence and financial stability.
georgia.benefits_after: Georgia's Independent Living Program serves eligible youth ages 14 to 21 with help for education, employment, housing, life skills, and adult connections, and youth who leave at 18 can return to extended care within six months. Former foster youth can keep Medicaid until age 26, apply for Education and Training Vouchers for college or job training, and may qualify for a state tuition and fee waiver at Technical College System of Georgia schools under O.C.G.A. § 20-3-660.
georgia.extended_care: Yes. Through the Connected by 21 / Extended Youth Support Services program, youth ages 18 to 21 who sign a voluntary placement agreement with DFCS can stay in foster care to age 21. They must be finishing high school or a GED, enrolled in college or vocational school, in a program that promotes or removes barriers to employment, working at least 120 hours a month (or 80 hours a month combined with school or another activity, or if a medical condition limits work), or unable to do those things because of a medical condition.
georgia.foster_overview: When a juvenile court judge finds a child cannot safely stay at home, the Georgia Division of Family and Children Services (DFCS) places the child in a foster home, with kin, or in another approved setting. Foster caregivers give the child a safe, stable home and daily care while DFCS works with the birth family toward reunification or another permanent plan.
georgia.kinship_care: Yes. DFCS looks for kinship care first when a child enters foster care, placing the child with a relative or fictive kin who has a long-standing bond with the child or family. Kinship caregivers get the same recruitment, training, and support as other caregivers, plus help from DFCS Caregiver Navigators, and can be approved by DFCS or a Child Placing Agency.
